appellant has preferred Criminal Appeal No.5399 of
2021, which is pending before the High Court. Along
with the Criminal Appeal, I.A. No.1715/2026 was
filed by the appellant for suspension of sentence
and for grant of bail. By the impugned order, I.A.
No.1715/2026 has been rejected.
6. This  Court  vide  order  dated  18.05.2026  had
issued notice pursuant to which respondent-State of
Madhya Pradesh has filed counter affidavit.
7. Learned Senior counsel for the appellant has
drawn the attention of the Court to the order dated
23.01.2026 passed by this Court in Special Leave
Petition (Criminal) No.16986 of 2025, whereby this
Court had granted bail to the co-convict Mangilal.
He further submits that three other accused persons
were acquitted by the Trial Court. Appellant has
already  undergone  more  than  08  years  of
incarceration. The appeal being of the year 2021,
is not likely to be heard by the High Court in the
2

## Page 218

near future. Therefore, the sentence imposed upon
the appellant  may be  suspended and  he may  be
enlarged on bail.
8. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent-
State of Madhya Pradesh submits that the High Court
has distinguished the role of the appellant from
that of co-convict Mangilal. He submits that it is
because of the assault by the appellant on the
victim with an iron rod that the victim passed
away. This would be evident from the medical report
and the evidence of the Doctor. He, therefore,
submits that the sentence qua the appellant may not
be suspended and he should not be enlarged on bail.
9. Responding to the above submission, learned

O R D E R  
1. Leave granted.  
2. The appellant is aggrieved by the final order dated 
03.12.2025 passed by the High Court of Judicature at 
Bombay, Bench at Aurangabad in Miscellaneous Civil 
Application No. 311 of 2024 whereby the High Court 
declined the appellant -wife's prayer seeking transfer of 
matrimonial proceedings from the Family Court at 
Aurangabad to the Family Court at Jalgaon.  
3. The brief facts giving rise to the present appeal are as 
follows: 
3.1. The marriage between the parties was solemnized 
in 2022 as per Hindu rites and ceremonies. 
Following the marriage, the parties resided together 
at Aurangabad.  
3.2. Matrimonial disputes subsequently arose between 
the parties. The respondent -husband instituted 

## Page 246

C.A.@ SLP(C.) NO.2879 OF 2026  2 
 
Petition No. A -570/2022 under Section 10 of the 
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 1 seeking judicial 
separation before the Family Court at Aurangabad, 
Maharashtra.  
3.3. The appellant instituted Petition No. A -176/2023 
under Section 9 of the Act for restitution of conjugal 
rights before the Family Court, Aurangabad, 
Maharashtra.  
3.4. FIR No.0143/2023 was registered at the instance 
of appellant’s father against the respondent and his 
family members under Sections 324, 323 504 and 
506 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 
1860.  
3.5. The respondent subsequently withdrew Petition 
No. A -570/2022 and instituted Petition No. A -
514/2023 under Section 13(1)(i -a) of the Act 
seeking divorce before the Family Court at 
Aurangabad.  
3.6. The appellant thereafter shifted to Jalgaon, where 
she presently resides. She also instituted 
proceedings under the Protection of Women from 
Domestic Violence Act, 2005 bearing PWDVA 
No.114/2024 before Judicial Magistrate First Class 
at Jalgaon. 
 
1 Hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’. 

## Page 247

C.A.@ SLP(C.) NO.2879 OF 2026  3 
 
3.7. By order dated 16.08.2024, the Family Court 
directed that Petition No. A -176 of 2023 and 
Petition No. A-514 of 2023 be tried together. 
3.8. Appellant filed Miscellaneous Civil Application No. 
311 of 2024 before the High Court seeking transfer 
of Petition No. A -176/2023 and Petition No. A -
514/2023 from the Family Court, Aurangabad to 
Family Court, Jalgaon.  
3.9. The High Court vide the impugned order dated 
03.12.2025 has declined to allow the transfer of 
matters.  
3.10. Aggrieved, the appellant is here before us.  
 
4. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the 
parties.  
5. The High Court declined the prayer for transfer primarily 
on the ground that the distance between Aurangabad and 
Jalgaon is approximately 160 kilometres. It observed that 
the appellant could participate in the proceedings 
through video conferencing. It further directed that if her 
physical presence was required before the Family Court 
at Aurangabad, the respondent shall pay a sum of 
Rs.3,000/- towards her travel and other expenses on 
each date of hearing. 

## Page 248

C.A.@ SLP(C.) NO.2879 OF 2026  4 
 
6. Having considered the material placed on record, we are 
of the considered view that the impugned order cannot be 
sustained for the reasons recorded hereinafter. 
7. Proceedings under the Domestic Violence Act, 2005 are 
already pending before the Judicial Magistrate First Class 
at Jalgaon. The appellant has also expressed an 
apprehension regarding her personal safety while 
travelling to Aurangabad. This apprehension is founded 
on an FIR registered against the respondent and his 
family members at the instance of the appellant's father. 
Without expressing any opinion on the merits of those 
allegations, we are of the view that these are relevant 
circumstances which required due consideration while 
deciding the prayer for transfer.  
8. The High Court instead proceeded on the premise that 
the availability of video conferencing and payment of 
travelling expenses would sufficiently address the 
appellant's concerns. It is not to say that these are not 
relevant considerations, however, they c annot by 
themselves be determinative of a prayer for transfer. The 
impugned order does not reflect any consideration of the 
cumulative effect of the circumstances noticed above. 
9. In the facts of the present case, we are satisfied that the 
interests of justice would be better served if the 
proceedings are allowed to be transferred. No substantial 
prejudice would be caused to the respondent if the 

## Page 249

C.A.@ SLP(C.) NO.2879 OF 2026  5 
 
proceedings are transferred to the Family Court at 
Jalgaon. 
10. Accordingly, the impugned order passed by the High 
Court is set aside. Petition No. A-176 of 2023 and Petition 
No. A-514/2023 are transferred from the Family Court, 
Aurangabad, Maharashtra to the Family Court, Jalgaon, 
Maharashtra. The parties are at liberty to appear through 
virtual mode.  
11. The appeal is allowed in the above terms. 
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Leave granted.
This  criminal  appeal  challenges  the  order  dated
25.07.2025 passed by the Bombay High Court in Interim
Application No. 989 of 2025 in Criminal Appeal No. 424 of
2022, whereby the appellant’s application for suspension
of sentence was dismissed. 
The appellant Mahendra Kesrinath Mestri faced trial
in connection with a crime registered pursuant to C.R No.
221/2013 dated 05.05.2013 lodged with P.S. Mahim, District
Mumbai  in  respect  of  the  offences  punishable  under
Sections 302 read with 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
(‘IPC’) and Sections 4 and 25 of the Arms Act, 1959.  
By judgment dated 21.10.2020 in Sessions Case No.
760/2013,  the  Additional  Sessions  Judge,  Gr.  Mumbai
convicted the appellant for the offence under Section 302
of the IPC and awarded a sentence of life imprisonment
1

## Page 261

along with a fine of Rs. 5000/- for the offence under
Section 302 of the IPC. 
The  appellant,  being  aggrieved  by  the  order  of
conviction passed by the trial court, filed Criminal
Appeal No. 424/2022 before the Bombay High Court and the
same is pending. During the pendency of the said criminal
appeal,  the  appellant  filed  Interim  Application  No.
989/2025 before the High Court seeking suspension of his
sentence. The High Court, by the impugned order dated
25.07.2025,  dismissed  the  application  filed  by  the
appellant for suspension of sentence. Hence, the present
criminal appeal. 
This Court, by order dated 17.08.2026, issued notice
in the instant matter.
We have heard the learned counsel in support of the
appellant and learned counsel for the respondent/State.
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that on
conviction under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the
IPC and Sections 4 and 25 of the Arms Act, 1959, the
appellant has been in jail between twelve to thirteen
years. The co-accused has been released on bail as there
is suspension of sentence in his case.  The  appeal filed
by the appellant is of the year 2022 and the adjudication
of the same by the High Court would inevitably take time.
2

## Page 262

Having regard to the long incarceration of the appellant,
this Court may consider suspending his sentence and
granting bail as the appellant has also a good case on
merits. In the circumstances,  the relief of suspension
of sentence and bail may be granted to the appellant
herein by setting aside the impugned order and allowing
this appeal. 
Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent/State,
submitted that there is no merit in this appeal.  The
appellant herein is the main accused. In case, the appeal
is not heard in time by the High Court, liberty is always
reserved to the appellant herein to seek remission of his
sentence and hence, this appeal may be dismissed.
Considering the facts on record, in our view, the
case for suspension of sentence is made out.
We, therefore, allow this appeal and direct as under:
“The  appellant  shall  be  produced  before  the
concerned trial Court as early as possible and the
trial Court shall release him on bail, subject to
such conditions as it may deem appropriate to
impose to ensure his presence in the concerned
proceedings.”
The appellant shall appear before the High Court as 
and when directed to do so.
3

## Page 263

It is directed that the appellant shall extend  
complete cooperation in the hearing of the appeal before 
the High Court. The appellant shall not misuse his  
liberty in any manner.
Any  infraction  of  the  conditions  may  entail  
cancellation of the suspension of sentence granted to the
appellant. 
With these observations, the criminal appeal is  
allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

CIVIL APPEAL NOS.          /2026
[@ SLP [C] NOS.13296-13297/2025]
DELHI DEVELOPMENT AUTHORITY            Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
SANJEET GAHLOT                          Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
We  have  heard  the  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the parties.
There are two issues raised before us.
One is with respect to the entitlement of the
respondent to a developed plot in Dwarka, and the
other  is  the  entitlement  of  the  respondent,
notwithstanding the seniority list.
On a perusal of the affidavits filed, it is
clear that a plot in Dwarka would not be available to
the respondent as a policy decision has been taken
not to allot plots in Dwarka to anyone including
those who are placed above the respondent in the
seniority list that has been drawn.  It has also been
brought to our notice that earlier, pursuant to a
direction of the High Court, three persons, who are
seniors to all the others, have been allotted plots
at Dwarka, through a special mini draw.

## Page 271

2
We are inclined to hold that the said act was
done in compliance with the order of the High Court,
which we find difficult to approve, but thereafter, a
policy decision has been taken in tune with the
seniority list.
We also take note of the fact that when the
earlier decision was taken, the plot in Dwarka was
underdeveloped.
Giving an alternative plot in pursuance of an
acquisition is a policy decision involving an element
of discretion. It was meant to give succor to the
erstwhile land owner who lost his land, apart from
the compensation which he received.
The same being a concession, power of judicial
review is rather limited. It can only be raised on
the touchstone of Article 14 of the Constitution of
India, 1950  inter  alia  contending that persons who
are junior to one seeking such allotment have been
granted as against him. That is not the case before
us.
Admittedly, the respondent before us is placed
at serial No.50 in the seniority list.  In other
words, 49 persons who are above the respondent also
lost their respective lands because of the same
acquisition  proceedings  pertaining  to  the  same
project.

## Page 272

3
In such view of the matter, we are not in a
position to give our imprimatur to the decision of
the High Court.
Even otherwise, the High Court ought not to have
undertaken such an exercise in contempt proceedings,
where issue is as to whether the decision of the
appellant is willful or contumacious.
In  such  view  of  the  matter,  the  impugned
order(s) stands set aside.
However, we make it clear that the respondent,
having contested the matter for quite a long time, is
entitled  to  an  expedited  process  of  alternative
allotment.  We expect such process to be completed
within a period of six months from the date of
receipt of a copy of this order.
The appellant shall make an endeavour to allot
plots situated at Narela, subject to availability and
seniority.

## Page 273

4
The appeals stand disposed of, accordingly.
Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The present petitions call in question the correctness of
the order dated 17-02-2026 in ABA No. 6888/2025 passed by the
High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi. By the said order, the
prayer for anticipatory bail of the petitioners were rejected
in connection with FIR No.60/2025 registered at Ghatshila
(Moubhandar),  Jamshedpur,  Jharkhand,  for  the  offences
punishable under Sections 318(4), 338, 336(3), 340, 115(2),
111(3), 351(2), 352 and 3(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,
2023.
2. When the matters came up for hearing on 23.04.2026 and
25.05.2026, this Court made the following orders:-
Order dated 23.04.2026
“1. Heard Mr. Jaspal Singh, learned counsel for the
petitioner.
2. Issue notice, returnable on 21st May, 2026.
3. In the meantime, in the event of arrest, the
petitioner shall be enlarged on bail subject to the
satisfaction of the Investigating Officer in connection
with  FIR  No.60/2025  registered  at  Ghatshila
(Moubhandar), Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, for the offences
punishable under Sections 318(4), 338, 336(3), 340,
115(2), 111(3), 351(2), 352 and 3(5) of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. The  petitioner,  however,  cooperate  in  the
investigation.
5. Call on 21st May, 2026.

## Page 309

3
Order dated 25.05.2026
1. Heard Mr. Jaspal Singh, learned counsel for the
petitioner.
2. Issue notice.
3. In the meantime, in the event of arrest, the
petitioner shall be enlarged on bail subject to the
satisfaction of the Investigating Officer in connection
with  FIR  No.60/2025  registered  at  Ghatshila
(Moubhandar), Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, for the offences
punishable under Sections 318(4), 338, 336(3), 340,
115(2), 111(3), 351(2), 352 and 3(5) of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. The petitioner is directed to appear before the
Investigating Officer on Friday, the 5 th June, 2026 and
join the investigation. The petitioner shall, however,
cooperate in the investigation.
5. Tag with SLP(Criminal)No.7185 of 2026.”
3. Today, we have heard Mr. Jaspal Singh, learned counsel
for the petitioners in both the petitions and Ms. Madhusmita
Bora, learned counsel and Mr.Venkat Narayan, learned counsel,
both appearing for the State.
4. It  is  not  disputed  that  both  the  petitioners  have
cooperated in the investigations.
5. Under the said fact and keeping the overall facts and
circumstances  of  the  cases,  we  confirm  the  orders  dated
23.04.2026  and  25.05.2026  passed  by  this  Court,  granting
interim protection to the petitioners.
6. With the above observations, the Special Leave Petitions
are disposed of.

ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Haryana.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
29.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.241/2025
registered  at  Police  Station-  Cyber  East,  District-
Gurugram, Haryana under Sections 318(4), 319(2), 204 and
61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (for short,
‘BNS’).
5. Case of the prosecution is that the complainant, an
elderly lady, was defrauded by the accused persons who
represented themselves as police officials from Mumbai,
1

## Page 324

falsely alleging that her name had appeared in a money
laundering case, whereafter she was induced to transfer
Rs.27,00,000/- from her HSBC bank account on 19.06.2025
and Rs.8,79,000/- from her Punjab & Sindh bank account on
20.06.2025 to the bank account of one Sumit Kumar Kashyap,
purportedly to extricate her from the so-called money
laundering case.
6. Appellant was arrested on 20.08.2025 and since then,
he has been in custody.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that there
are altogether five accused. The main accused Sumit Kumar
Kashyap has been granted bail by the Trial Court. 03 other
accused persons have been granted bail by the High Court.
Only the appellant has been left out. She submits that
given  the  facts  and  circumstances,  appellant  may  be
enlarged on bail.
8. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Haryana,
on the other hand, has referred to the counter affidavit
filed on behalf of the respondent-State of Haryana and
submits that appellant has another criminal antecedent of
similar nature and is in custody in the said case arising
out of FIR No.37/2025. According to him, appellant is the
mastermind and, therefore, he may not be enlarged on bail.
9. Replying to the above submissions, learned counsel
for the appellant submits that appellant has been added as
an accused and arrested following the disclosure statement
of other accused persons. No money has been deposited into
2

## Page 325

his bank account or recovered from him. Insofar FIR
No.37/2025 is concerned, appellant has been granted bail
by the Trial Court on 11.12.2025. It was only when he was
in custody in the aforesaid case that the appellant came
to be implicated in the present case.
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that a case for
grant of bail is made out.
11. Having regard to the above, the impugned order dated
29.05.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  is  set  aside.
Consequently,  we  direct  that  the  appellant  shall  be
produced before the Trial Court within a maximum period of
07 days from today, whereafter he shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed
appropriate.
12. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.

of.

Leave granted.
This appeal challenges the judgment and order dated 
04.05.2026 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana
at Chandigarh in CRM-M No. 1368 of 2026 (O&M).
The appellant has been facing trial in connection
with crime registered pursuant to FIR No. 181/2025 dated
15.10.2025 registered with P.S. Dakha, District Ludhiana
Rural, State Punjab in respect of offences punishable
under  Sections  140(1),  319(2),  308(5),  3(5)  of  the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita,2023 (“BNS”).
An application for regular bail of the appellant
having been disallowed by the High Court vide impugned
order  dated  04.05.2026,  the  appellant  is  before  us
against the same by way of this appeal.
This Court, vide  its order dated 27.05.2026, had
issued notice in the instant matter.
1

## Page 328

We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and 
learned counsel for the State and perused the material 
on record. 
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the
State has not been serious  in apprehending two main accused,
namely, Aman and Vinay, who are still absconding.  However,
the appellant has been in jail since 17.10.2025. The charges
have been framed but the trial is yet to commence.  There are
as many as 24 witnesses and inevitably the trial will be
prolonged.  In the circumstances, this Court may set aside the
impugned order and grant the relief of bail subject to the
conditions to be imposed.
Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent/State,
with reference to the counter affidavit contented that
there are criminal antecedents as against the  appellant
herein; that the State is endeavoring to secure the other
two accused, who are absconding; that there is another co-
accused Gurwinder Singh, who is also in custody. In the
circumstances, having regard to the seriousness of the
offences alleged against the appellant herein,  the appeal
may be dismissed.
  Considering the facts on record, in our view, the
case for bail is made out.
    We, therefore, allow this appeal and direct as  
2

## Page 329

under:
“The appellant shall be produced before the
concerned trial Court as early as possible
and the trial Court shall release him on
bail, subject to such conditions as it may
deem appropriate to impose to ensure his
presence in the proceedings arising out of
FIR No. 181/2025  mentioned above.”
  It is directed that the appellant shall extend
complete cooperation in the trial of the instant case.
The appellant shall not misuse his liberty in any manner.
 Any  infraction  of  the  conditions  may  entail  
cancellation of bail granted to the appellant.
 With these observations, the appeal is allowed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
  CIVIL APPEAL NO.3602/2011
PARKASH CHAND & ORS.                     Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
GIAN CHAND (DEAD) THR LRS & ORS.        Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. The present appeal has been filed against the
impugned judgment dated 18.12.2009, passed by the
High  Court  of  Himachal  Pradesh  in  R.S.A.
No.377/2006,  wherein,  the  suit  for  permanent
injunction filed by the appellant(s) was dismissed
and the findings rendered in the judgements passed
by  the  Trial  Court  dated  27.04.2005  and  First
Appellate Court dated 12.01.2006 were affirmed.
2. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the parties.
3. The appellant(s) in the present case, are the
plaintiffs in the suit. The suit has been filed by
the plaintiffs claiming to be co-sharers in the suit
properties,  seeking  the  relief  of  permanent
injunction  to  restrain  the  respondent(s)  from
raising any constructions over the suit lands.

## Page 336

2
4. Before the Trial Court, the respondent(s) took
the plea of adverse possession to claim their title.
Incidentally, a judgment between the respondent(s)
and another co-sharer of same suit land was relied
upon, indicating that the possession vested with the
respondent(s). All the Courts below have dismissed
the suit by placing reliance upon the factum of
possession in an earlier suit which was decreed in
favour of predecessor of the respondents/defendants,
where the appellant(s) were not made a party.
5. On  facts,  it  is  not  in  dispute  that  the
respondent(s) have put up certain constructions. The
respondent(s) have also taken the plea of adverse
possession, which has not been taken note of by the
Courts themselves, as they have relied solely upon
the judgment passed in an earlier suit. Law is quite
settled that the right to title is different from a
suit for injunction. The relevant factors to be
considered in a suit for injunction pertain to the
factum of possession and the nature of an act which
has been carried out by the respondent(s). Suffice
it is to state, that respondent(s) have put up
constructions over the suit properties.
6. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to
hold that the present proceedings would not bar the
appellant(s) to file a suit seeking a comprehensive

## Page 337

3
prayer for the declaration of title.  
7. Accordingly, the appeal stands disposed of by
giving liberty to the appellant(s) to file a fresh
suit for the declaration of title.
8. In the event of such a suit being filed for
declaration of title and for consequential relief of
possession by the appellant(s), the earlier suit
filed inter se  the parties, along with the findings
therein  shall  not  stand  in  the  way  of  fresh
proceedings instituted by the appellant(s).
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

1. Heard Mr. Abhimanyu Tewari, learned counsel for the
petitioners Mr. Divyanshu Rai, learned counsel for the defacto

## Page 344

2
complainant and Mr. Kapil Balwani, learned counsel for the
State.
2. The present petition calls in question the correctness of
the order dated 05-05-2026 in CRMM No. 59830/2025 passed by the
High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh. By the said
order, the High Court allowed the complainant’s application and
set aside the orders dated 09.09.2025 and 15.09.2025 granting
interim  protection  to  the  petitioners  and  subsequently
confirming the same by the Additional Sessions Judge, Mansa,
Punjab (for short, ‘ASJ at Mansa’).
3. When the matter came up for hearing on 22.05.2026, this
Court, while issuing notice, stayed the operation of the
impugned order.
4. The  case  arose  out  of  an  FIR  No.235/2025  dated
14.08.2025, inter alia, against the petitioners, registered at
Police Station Sadar Mansa, District Mansa, Punjab for the
offences punishable under Sections 318(2), 336(2), 336(3), 338,
340(2), 316, 319, 61(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
and Sections 66(C) ad 66(D) of the Information Technology Act,
2000. It is not disputed that ASJ at Mansa on 09.09.2025
granted  interim  protection  and  confirmed  the  same  on
15.09.2025.
5. While confirming the anticipatory bail, the Trial Judge
recorded the following findings, which are as under:-
“…..It is also the fact that accused/applicants
acquired about 40 acres of land. There is
nothing brought on the record at this stage
regarding the fact that there is any such
involvement of accused/applicants in duping the

## Page 345

3
complainant for huge amount as alleged in the
FIR.  Accused/applicants  have  joined  the
investigation. So, the present bail application
is  allowed  and  the  interim  order  dated
09.09.2025 is made absolute. Further directions
are issued to the accused/applicants that they
will appear before the investigating officer as
and when called by the investigating officer
and they will not leave the country without the
prior permission of ld. Illaqa Magistrate, the
applicants shall not induce/threat any of the
prosecution  witnesses  or  tamper  with  the
evidence in any manner and the applicants shall
appear on each and every date of hearing of the
court.  Record  of  the  bail  application  be
consigned to record room.”
6. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and
perusing the records, we are satisfied that no case for setting
aside of the orders of ASJ at Mansa, granting anticipatory bail
as early as on 15.09.2025, was made out. As to their role, if
any, in duping the complainant and the nexus between the money
received and the conspiracy, are all matters to be decided at
the trial. The petitioners having had benefit of interim
protection from 09.09.2025, there was no justification on facts
for the High Court to set aside the order granting the said
interim protection.
7. The ASJ at Mansa having enlarged the petitioners on
anticipatory bail, no convincing reasons have been assigned by
the High Court for setting aside the impugned order.
8. We, for the reasons stated above, set aside the impugned
order of the High Court dated 05.05.2026. The consequence will
be that the petitioners will continue to have the interim
protection as originally granted on 09.09.2025 and confirmed on
15.09.2025 by the ASJ at Mansa. However, the observation made

## Page 346

4
herein are only for the purpose of deciding the present special
leave petition and the trial and other proceedings will proceed
uninfluenced by the observations in the impugned order as well
as in the present order. 
9. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the above
terms.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

come in the way or influence/prejudice the case of the petitioner
during the trial or in any subsequent proceeding.
3. We find the prayer to be bona fide.

been made in the order dated 24.04.2026, being only for the
purposes of considering the cancellation of bail granted to the
applicant-respondent No.2 shall not cause prejudice to him either
in the trial or in any subsequent proceedings.
5. IA No. 166471/2026 , application for clarification is allowed
in the aforementioned terms.
6. Consequently, the Miscellaneous Application stands disposed
of.

1. Delay condoned.

## Page 385

3. It seems to us that the liberty granted by this Court vide the
order dated 05.01.2026 in SLP(C) No.34/2026 provides sufficient
protection to the aggrieved villagers/Gram Panchayats to approach
the Competent Authority in order to safeguard their constitutional
rights.
4. In view of the above, no further interference is warranted in
the impugned order passed by the High Court of Judicature for
Rajasthan at Jodhpur.
5. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
6. All pending application(s), if any, also stand disposed of.
SLP(C) No. 27647/2026
7. The petitioners’ village, i.e. Narpara, was demerged from Gram
Panchayat Noon and was merged with Gram Panchayat Sarat  vide
notification dated 21.11.2025. That notification was reversed on
28.12.2025,  thereby  retaining  the  village  Narpara  with  Noon.
However, within 48 hours, another notification came on 31.12.2025,
reversing the notification dated 28.12.2025, and reinstating the
merger with Sarat.
8. As a consequence, the notification dated 21.11.2025 became
operative once again. The petitioners challenged the notification
dated 31.12.2025, but the High Court has declined to interfere on
the ground that similar notifications pertaining to other Gram
Panchayats have already been upheld by a Coordinate Bench. The
aggrieved petitioners are before this Court.
9. Whether  the  village  Narpara  should  be  merged  with  Gram
Panchayat Noon or with Gram Panchayat Sarat is essentially a policy
2

## Page 386

matter. If the petitioners have any valid grievance against such
merger or demerger, liberty is granted to them to approach the
competent Authority against the notification dated 31.12.2025. We
have  no  reason  to  doubt  that  such  representation  shall  be
objectively considered by the competent Authority in accordance
with  law.  Let  an  appropriate  decision  be  taken  on  the
representation preferably within three months.
10. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
11. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

1. Heard Mr. Jitendra Bharti learned counsel appearing
for the petitioner and Mr. B.Karunakarn, learned standing
counsel appearing for the respondent-State, on advance
notice.
SLP (Criminal) No.8859/2026 Page 1 of 3

## Page 391

2. The  present  petition  calls  in  question  the
correctness of the order dated 6 th February, 2026 passed
by the High Court of Judicature at Madras in CRLOP No.
2740/2026.  By the said order, the High Court has denied
the benefit of bail to the petitioner.
3. We  have  carefully  considered  the  records  and
perused the counter affidavit of the respondent-State.
It is not disputed that the petitioner is in custody for
more than one year.
4. The only apprehension expressed by the respondent-
State is that the petitioner belongs to another State.
Learned counsel for the petitioner however undertakes
that a condition can be imposed that the petitioner will
not leave the State of Tamil Nadu till the conclusion of
the trial.
5. Considering the facts and circumstances, the period
undergone and likelihood of time that will be taken for
completion of the trial, the fact that the trail has not
even  commenced  and  keeping  in  mind  the  principles
enshrined in Article 21 of the Constitution of India as
well as the twin conditions of Section 37 of the Narcotic
Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 , we are
inclined to enlarge the petitioner on bail, pending
trial.
SLP (Criminal) No.8859/2026 Page 2 of 3

## Page 392

6. We direct that pending trial, the petitioner shall
be enlarged on bail subject to the satisfaction of the
Trial Court.  
7. The Trial Court shall, however, impose as one of
the conditions,  a condition  to the  effect that  the
petitioner shall not leave the boundaries of the State of
Tamil Nadu till the completion of the trial apart from
other conditions, it may choose to impose.
8. The Special Leave Petition is disposed of in the
above terms.
9. Pending applications shall also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Exemption Application is allowed.
2. We heard this matter for quite some time.
3. Mr. Naveen Pahwa, the learned Senior Counsel appeared on
behalf of the State of Himachal Pradesh, Mr. Siddharth Aggarwal,
the learned Senior Counsel appeared on behalf of the Respondent
Nos.1 and 4 respectively and Mr. Karan Bhardwaj, the learned
counsel appeared for the Respondent Nos.2 and 3 respectively.
3. We take notice of the fact that Respondent No.1 is the
original borrower. Respondent No.4 happens to be the son of
Respondent No. 1. Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 respectively are Bank
Officers alleged to have been involved in the fraud highlighted by
the State.
4. Having heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
parties and having gone through the materials on record, we are of
the view that the presence of the Bank is necessary before us.
5. The learned Advocate-on-Record appearing for the State shall
implead Kangra Central Co-operative Bank as party Respondent No.5.
6. The cause title be amended accordingly. 
7. Let notice be issued to the Bank, returnable on 31-8-2026.
8. In the course of today's hearing, we put few questions to the
learned Senior Counsel appearing for the State, more particularly,
what is the amount due and payable by the original borrower to the
Bank with interest as on date. We also enquired with the learned
Senior Counsel about the security interest created at the time of
disbursement of the loan amounts over a period of time. 
9. The learned Senior Counsel appearing for the original borrower
would submit that his client has created security interest over two
parcels  of  land  valued  at  more  than  Rs.150  Crore.
10. We would like to know from the Bank, by way of an affidavit,
duly affirmed by a responsible Bank Officer, as regards the exact
amount due and payable by the original borrower to the Bank with
interest, and also details of the security interest said to have
been created by the borrower over two plots of land as referred to

## Page 410

3
above.
11. The Bank should also place on record the 13(2) SARFAESI
Notices, if issued, so that we can look into the same to ascertain
what type of security interest has been created. 
12. By the next date of hearing, the Bank shall also place on
record  before  us  the  Valuation  Certificate  issued  by  two
Government-approved valuers insofar as the two plots offered by the
borrower by way of security is concerned.
13. We would like to know from the Bank what steps it took
departmentally against the Respondent Nos.2 and 3 respectively. Why
the Bank allowed Respondent No.2 to retire? Why Respondent No.3 as
on date is still serving with the Bank despite the fact that
serious  allegations  of  fraud  have  been  leveled  against  him?
14. We would also like to know from the Bank in what manner over a
period  of  time,  the  Board  of  Directors  looked  into  these
transactions and how they were dealt with. We are conscious of the
fact that the Board of Directors have also been arrayed as accused
persons.  However,  as  informed  by  the  learned  Senior  Counsel
appearing for the Bank, they were issued with Section 41A notice
under the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. They appeared before
the Investigating Officer in pursuance of such notice, and after
interrogation, the Investigating Officer did not deem fit to effect
any arrest.
15. The affidavit of the Bank should indicate how the Board of
Directors sanctioned the loan over a period of time. The affidavit
should be explicit insofar as the bye-laws of the Society are
concerned and the sanctioning authority.

## Page 421

2
Court has wrongly applied the law laid down
in the case of  State of Punjab & Ors. vs.
Rafiq Masih (White Washer) and Ors. (2015 4
SCC  334)  inasmuch  as  Rafiq  Masih  (supra)
concerns  recovery  made  from  a  lowly  paid
employee after his superannuation when excess
payment was made concerning the pay scale,
increment etc; and where the employee has not
committed  any  fraud  or  concealment  in
securing such excess payment. Where as, in
the case at hand, the respondent was posted
at Dehradun, Uttarakhand and was transferred
to Tehri, Uttarakhand however, he continued
to  retain  his  quarter  at  Dehradun,
Uttarakhand and got another quarter at Tehri,
Uttarakhand.  Respondent,  while  securing
allotment  of  quarter  at  Dehradun,
Uttarakhand,  did  not  disclose  that  he  is
already  retaining  a  quarter  at  Dehradun,
Uttarakhand.
3. Issue notice.
4. Mr.  Anurag,  learned  AOR,  appears;
accepts  notice  for  the  respondent  and
undertakes to file counter affidavit within
four weeks.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The  present  Special  Leave  Petition  calls  in
question the correctness of the judgment dated 7 th May,
2026 passed by the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at
Amaravati in Commercial Court Appeal No.27 of 2025.  By
1

## Page 457

the said judgment, the High Court reversed the order of
the Commercial Court and held that the Court at Vizag,
Visakhapatnam would have jurisdiction to hear the Section
9 application after harmoniously construing Clauses 57
and 58 of the contract in question.
2. When the matter came up before this Court, we put
it to the parties that a better course of action will be
to have an Arbitrator appointed so that the parties could
invoke Section 17 of the Arbitration and Conciliation
Act, 1996 before the Arbitrator.  Both the parties have
favourably responded to the suggestion of the Court.  The
parties consented to the appointment of a sole Arbitrator
to adjudicate the disputes between them arising out of
the contract in question.  The parties agree that the
sole Arbitrator would adjudicate all disputes arising
between the parties.
3. Considering the developments before us and with the
consent of both the parties, we appoint Justice Ramesh
Ranganathan, former Chief Justice of the Uttarakhand High
Court and former Chairman of the Appellate Tribunal for
Electricity to act as a sole Arbitrator to adjudicate the
disputes between the parties.
4. The parties shall get in touch with the learned
Arbitrator to carry the matter forward.  The fees and
other terms shall be fixed in consultation with the
learned Arbitrator.
2

## Page 458

5. At  this  stage,  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
petitioner submits that liberty may be given to the
parties to treat the Section 9 pleadings as pleadings
under Section 17 before the learned Arbitrator.
6. We grant liberty to the petitioner to make a prayer
before the learned Arbitrator.
7. A copy of this order shall be forwarded to Justice
Ramesh  Ranganathan,  f ormer  Chief  Justice  of  the
Uttarakhand  High  Court  and  former  Chairman  of  the
Appellate Tribunal for Electricity.
8. With  the  above  observations,  the  Special  Leave
Petition is disposed of.
9. The order passed under Section 9 petition shall
continue  to  operate  till  such  time  the  Section  17
petition is decided.
10. Pending application shall also stand disposed of.
(ANITA MALHOTRA)                          (MANOJ KUMAR)
     DEPUTY REGISTRAR                          COURT MASTER

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Mr. Kapil Sibal, learned senior counsel for the appellant
submitted that I.A. No. 254594 of 2026, an application seeking
exemption  from  surrender  be  listed  before  the  Court  on
1

## Page 592

31.08.2026. 
2. On  the  other  hand,  Mr.  Tushar  Mehta,  learned  Solicitor
General, opposed the aforesaid prayer and pointed out that
Order XX Rule 3 of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013 is mandatory
in nature, in view of which, until and unless the appellant
surrenders, the appeal cannot be listed before the Court. In
support of the aforesaid submission, reliance has been placed
on a decision of this Court 1. However, it is fairly submitted
that the Court has power to do away with the requirement of
surrender. 
3. A Two-Judge Bench of this Court 2 while considering Order XXI
Rule 13-A of Supreme Court Rules, 1966 (since repealed) which
is in pari materia with Order XX Rule 3 of the Supreme Court
Rules, 2013 has held the same to be mandatory. Therefore,
until  and  unless,  suitable  orders  are  passed  on  the
application  seeking  exemption  from  surrender,  the  appeal
cannot be listed before the Court. Therefore, the prayer made
to list the matter before the Court without considering the
application  seeking  exemption  from  surrender,  cannot  be
accepted. 
4. Mr. Kapil Sibal, learned senior counsel has not addressed this
Court on the merits of the application seeking exemption from
surrender. With a view to afford him an opportunity to address
the  Court  on  the  aforesaid  I.A.,  list  the  same  for
consideration on 25.08.2026.
(KANCHAN CHOUHAN)                            (PARVEEN KUMAR RAWAT)

1.  We have heard Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, learned Additional

## Page 670

2
Solicitor General of India, who vehemently contends that the High
Court has not considered the statutory bar as contained in Section
43(D) of the UAPA Act.  However, keeping in view the peculiar facts
and circumstances of this case, we are not inclined to interfere
with the impugned order, especially in light of the following
reason.
2.  In the event, the respondent is found involved in influencing
the witnesses and/or impeding the pending trial, it will be treated
as a misuse of concession of bail and upon application by the
State, the High Court will re-consider the impugned order.
(i) The  NIA has  already  examined  several  sensitive
witnesses qua the respondent; and
(ii) By an earlier order, this Court gave liberty to
renew the bail prayer after six months. 
3.     We also deem it appropriate to add that the application for
bail of the co-accused persons shall be decided by the concerned
Court as per their own merit without being influenced by the
impugned order passed by the High Court.
2. With  these  observations,  the  Special  Leave  Petition
stands disposed of.

the trial had commenced. Such observation is found
